text:
The premise is false. Evidence is mixed: the best randomized trial of hybrid work (Bloom et al., *Nature*, 2024, Trip.com) found no productivity or promotion penalty and about a third lower attrition. A board member who knows that study will discredit a memo claiming consensus.

A defensible version is that fully remote work carries productivity risks in some settings. Three bullets you can support, with the studies from memory, so verify figures before citing:

- **Output drops in some fully remote roles.** Atkin, Schoar & Shinde (2023) found data-entry workers in India were about 18% less productive fully remote. Gibbs, Mengel & Siemroth (2023) found IT professionals at an Asian firm were roughly 8-19% less productive working from home, despite longer hours.
- **Remote work weakens mentoring and learning.** Emanuel, Harrington & Pallais found software engineers who sat near teammates got more feedback, and the loss from remote work falls hardest on junior staff. This is a long-term cost that short-run output metrics miss.
- **Remote work hurts collaborative and unstructured work more than routine tasks.** This is an inference from the above, not a measured consensus. It argues for in-person time for training, onboarding, and cross-team work rather than a blanket ban.

The strongest case against your position is that hybrid arrangements and some fully remote ones (Bloom's 2015 call-center study, +13%) show neutral or positive effects. If your firm's work is mostly independent and measurable, the evidence favors flexibility. Anchor the memo in your own performance data, not a claim of consensus.
